content:
And that's...fascinating.

Disabling Cardbook does indeed restore the calendar, data fully intact, and that's excellent.

That does, however, raise a couple of other questions - neither as immediately pressing, but which the code-wranglers (and documentation folk) among us may want to address in the near term.

First, I'm also using an add-on/extension from Thunderbird Services called "Add-on compatibility check", which "Checks all installed add-ons for compatibility with Thunderbird ESR (yearly updates) and Thunderbird Release (monthly updates)."...and which currently still shows CardBook as compatible with both 153 (ESR) and 159 (Release). This is not *entirely* surprising...if I read the tea leaves correctly, the update that killed CardBook's compatibility went live just within the last couple of days, and the compatibility extension may itself need an update in order to catch the specific bug. [I note here that it has one other extension I'd installed marked as incompatible with 159 and disabled - PrintingTools NG - but I don't recall that one having caused anything like the catastrophic failure CardBook seems to have produced.]

Second, and possibly more significant:

Disabling CardBook does seem to have slightly tweaked the interface of the Advanced Settings dialog/screen when I go back and look - but that screen still does *not* fully match the description given in the support article I found on my first pass through Mozilla Support and discussed above. There's still nothing on that screen labeled Config Editor, and without poking closely I don't see anywhere for a Reset toggle to live. That suggests to me that changes have been made in the Advanced Settings interface since that article was written (or last updated), and if that's the case then the support article should be updated to reflect those changes.

The interesting thing about that support article, though, is that it describes what happened to me (and to LouH) so very closely - and that disabling CardBook worked so very efficiently as to produce exactly the effect the article describes. *That* suggests to me that whatever is presently wrong with CardBook has something to do with precisely whatever it is that the line of settings information in the support article was designed to control. And in turn, that the CardBook programmers should therefore be looking at that article and the relevant line of code as they attempt to stamp out the present bug.
